channel.title: grime95! — one booking a day
channel.description: Serialized small-town fiction: the Ponder County Sheriff's booking records for Saturday, December 2, 1995. One new booking every day at noon Eastern. All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0267 — Crystal Vanderpool: Retrieving a Polaroid (her own); it's evidence; it's on the Sheriff's desk
item.description: At 10:30 Saturday morning Sheriff Ponder booked Crystal Vanderpool for asking him to dinner at the Rexall in front of Bob. Wrote solicitation; no box for the other thing. Took her Polaroid, put it on his desk, called it evidence. Bonita Escobedo read it off his palm at nine that night. At 1:15 a.m. Crystal came back for her picture.
item.content:encoded:
At 10:30 Saturday morning Sheriff Ponder booked Crystal Vanderpool for asking him to dinner at the Rexall in front of Bob. Wrote solicitation; no box for the other thing. Took her Polaroid, put it on his desk, called it evidence. Bonita Escobedo read it off his palm at nine that night. At 1:15 a.m. Crystal came back for her picture.

Twenty-eight, long blonde hair showing roots, feathered bangs, pale blue shirt open over white, hoop earrings, fine chain. Eyes wide, mouth open, always looking like she'd just heard something. Through the courthouse's black-framed doors she came like she owned a piece of it. Might could make a case.

“I want my picture.”

“It's evidence, Crystal.”

“Of WHAT?”

He didn't have that. Man could find a charge easier than a dinner reservation.

“Marvin. Is it on your DESK?”

“That's where evidence goes.”

“Evidence goes in a damn BOX.”

“Some of it goes on the desk.”

“Then it's a picture of me on your desk.”

Sure as shit, it was. Bless them both. One asking for supper and the other trying to process the invitation through county government.

He booked her for retrieving it because he couldn't book himself for keeping it. Wide-eyed, animated in the second Polaroid, at the front doors, having said the true thing where everybody could hear. Hell of a witness.

The first one's still on the desk. She's never gotten it back. She's stopped asking. She comes by.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0072 — Eugene Halvorsen "The Editor": Interference with an investigation (asking questions); freedom of the press, contested
item.description: Eugene Halvorsen edits the Ponder County Ledger. Comes out Thursdays. At noon Saturday he was at his desk in a faded tee, with a Coke and a bemused look. Bethany Kuhn, the community columnist, had called at eleven.
item.content:encoded:
Eugene Halvorsen edits the Ponder County Ledger. Comes out Thursdays. At noon Saturday he was at his desk in a faded tee, with a Coke and a bemused look. Bethany Kuhn, the community columnist, had called at eleven.

"Eugene, get down to the jail."

"Bethany, it's Saturday."

"That's the story."

He stayed put. The Sheriff came to him, accidentally. Headed to the Rexall for film because Dwight had used every damn bit. Eugene waved him in past the Ledger window.

"Marvin, sit down. What the hell is going on?"

The Sheriff sat. Eugene asked eleven questions; got four answers. Gordon, his assistant, typed. Gray hair, blue shirt, other man in the frame. Not booked. Merely employed, though the distinction was getting thin.

"You can't print this, Eugene."

"It's a newspaper."

"It's a Saturday."

"That's what Bethany said."

The Sheriff booked him right at his desk. For asking. He ain't proud. Says the Ledger would've printed the cow, and the cow "didn't need that." Well, shit. A free press had run up against livestock privacy.

Eugene's leaning on the desk in the Polaroid, glasses, Coke, that look. He came to jail later, saw the pile, printed none of it. Decent man. Knows these folks have to buy groceries after Thursday.

Says he's "holding it for the right week." Thirty years. Still holding it.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0071 — DeShawn Pickett "DJ Pick": Noise violation; operating a sound system from a moving vehicle in a parade (unregistered entry)
item.description: The Ponder County Christmas Parade had forty-one registered entries and DeShawn Pickett. His Cutlass, two fifteens in the trunk, fell in behind Santa's tractor at 9:15 and stayed. Registration apparently hadn't covered a man bringing his own damn thunder.
item.content:encoded:
The Ponder County Christmas Parade had forty-one registered entries and DeShawn Pickett. His Cutlass, two fifteens in the trunk, fell in behind Santa's tractor at 9:15 and stayed. Registration apparently hadn't covered a man bringing his own damn thunder.

He called it “a mix.” It was Bone Thugs. Forty feet ahead, the high school band played “Joy to the World.” They fought eleven blocks. The band lost. Fifteen-year-olds against fifteens ain't a fair fight; one side's got homework.

Reserve Deputy Toad waved him out at Church Street. DeShawn waved back. Friendly as hell. At Oak, Toad tried again and DeShawn turned it up. Some folks can't hear authority without more bass.

Toad gave up and marched. Says he “kind of got into it.” God love him, if your parade's getting hijacked, might as well find the beat.

They finally booked DeShawn at noon at the Legion, where the parade ended, after he'd played the whole crowd out of their cars. Grinning in the Polaroid, one eye squinted, red jersey saying HIP HOP. No bullshit about what department he represented.

“I was the closer.”

The band director filed the complaint. The band didn't. The band wants him back next year. Hell, they know when they've got a good closer.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0070 — Vince Corrado: Receiving and concealing stolen property (one nacho cart, in transit)
item.description: Dwight took exactly one Polaroid outside. The nacho cart wouldn't fit through the door, and hell, even our jail has limits.
item.content:encoded:
Dwight took exactly one Polaroid outside. The nacho cart wouldn't fit through the door, and hell, even our jail has limits.

That's Vince Corrado in the car: cap, mustache, burgundy pants, forearm tattoo of a woman who left. His brother-in-law Mitch is standing over him in glasses and a black jacket. Mitch ain't under arrest. Mitch is just always there, like the extra bolt after you fix something.

At noon Deputy Hargrove found Tammy Jo Carter's stolen bingo-hall nacho cart in the bed of Vince's Datsun at the Gas-N-Go. It was plugged into the outdoor outlet beside the ice machine. Cheese at temperature. Whatever else Vince was doing wrong, he wasn't serving folks cold goddamn nachos.

“Tammy Jo asked me to hold it,” Vince said.

“You're selling out of it.”

“Still holding it. Ain't let it go nowhere.”

He'd sold nineteen orders to the parade crowd at two dollars apiece. That, he explained, was “separate.” A fine distinction if your bookkeeping consists of two pants pockets.

God love him, Vince would keep the cheese hot through a bankruptcy. Doesn't make the shit legal, but it does make lunch.

Mitch said nothing. He was holding a tire gauge. Nobody knows why.

The cart moved on. It always does.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0069 — Landon Meeks: Vandalism (Sunset Lanes, shoe rental); took shoes to the parade
item.description: Landon Meeks is nineteen and he went to the Christmas parade in bowling shoes. Bowling shoes. In the sleet. God love him, the boy's dumber than a bag of hammers and twice as sweet.
item.content:encoded:
Landon Meeks is nineteen and he went to the Christmas parade in bowling shoes. Bowling shoes. In the sleet. God love him, the boy's dumber than a bag of hammers and twice as sweet.

Sunset Lanes rental shoes. Red and blue. Size 11, with the 11 on the heel. He'd been at open bowling Friday night and walked out in 'em and nobody stopped him, and he figured Saturday morning that they were the only clean shoes he owned and a parade was a nice occasion.

He stood on the curb in front of the Rexall in a Nike tank over a white tee and an LA cap and rental shoes, and watched Santa go by and the Shriners and DeShawn Pickett's Cutlass with the fifteens rattling the Rexall windows, and them shoes were on the wet sidewalk the whole while, which is the one thing about bowling shoes: you cannot do that. The soles just go.

The man who owns Sunset Lanes was at the parade too. He looked down.

"Son, those are mine."

"Hell, I'm bringin' 'em back."

"They're WET, Landon. They're soaked through. You've ruint 'em. Those are eleven-dollar shoes, you little shit."

"They're real comfortable, though."

"Well, they WOULD be. They're bowling shoes."

Hargrove booked him for the shoes because the owner stood there till he did. Landon's got a little half-smile in the Polaroid, lips parted, the cap. Standing next to him with a mustache and a face is a man nobody has ever identified -- not booked, not named, just in the frame, God knows why -- and Dwight didn't crop him and Landon swears he don't know him and the man says nothing because he's a Polaroid.

The shoes went back. The soles were gone. Landon owes eleven dollars and is paying it a dollar a week, in person, every Friday, and then he bowls. Owner says he's gotten pretty good. Says he's got the shoes for it.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0068 — Stacy Delgado: Accessory (poinsettias); aiding a romantic gesture
item.description: Stacy Delgado loves her brother Ronnie Delgado enough to help him and not quite enough to keep her mouth shut afterward. That's family, sure as shit.
item.content:encoded:
Stacy Delgado loves her brother Ronnie Delgado enough to help him and not quite enough to keep her mouth shut afterward. That's family, sure as shit.

She works the counter at Ponder Floral & Gift. At 11:30 that morning she told Ronnie on the phone the loading dock “wasn't locked till five.” He stole sixty poinsettias off it at 4:45 that afternoon. Stacy got booked before he did. Around here we can be ahead of schedule in the worst damn ways.

Deputy Stotts came in at 11:40 about something else: the wreaths Hank Oberlin bought for the VFW came from Ponder Floral, and the invoice needed explaining. Stacy, striped top and red lipstick, volunteered, “If this is about Ronnie, I didn't tell him anything.”

“What about Ronnie?”

“Nothing.”

“Stacy.”

“He's got a girl in Sedalia. It's a whole thing. He's fine. He hasn't done it yet.”

Hell of a defense. The crime was still fixin' to happen and already had a witness statement.

Stotts wrote it down and waited. At 4:45, Ronnie did it. Stacy's neutral in the Polaroid, dark eyes under the shadow bands from the blinds. She ain't proud of the paperwork, but she isn't withdrawing her support for her brother, either. That's a sister for you.

She says she's not sorry. Denise didn't deserve him. Denise, reached in Sedalia, agreed.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0067 — Jeremy Fusco: Puppetry without consent; harassment of a Santa
item.description: Jeremy Fusco brought his own puppet to sit on Walmart Santa's lap. Nineteen years old, and apparently the regular line wasn't enough trouble without carry-on baggage.
item.content:encoded:
Jeremy Fusco brought his own puppet to sit on Walmart Santa's lap. Nineteen years old, and apparently the regular line wasn't enough trouble without carry-on baggage.

The doll was named Bucky. Had a face like he'd heard something through the bathroom wall and was saving it for supper. Jeremy waited forty minutes with him on his arm, then set him on Santa's knee and started making requests in Bucky's voice.

Bucky wanted a lot. Specific things about Santa's marriage. Things you don't put in a damn letter unless you want a lawyer answering it.

Walmart Santa, also the mail carrier, lasted two minutes. Give the man that. Then he grabbed Bucky by the head, Jeremy grabbed Santa by the beard, and off came the beard. Eleven children learned something a hell of a lot earlier than scheduled.

Deputy Hargrove booked Jeremy with Bucky in his lap because the boy wouldn't let go. Bless his heart, Jeremy would take a charge before he'd abandon his little troublemaker. Loyalty's worth something, even when it's attached to bullshit.

In the Polaroid Jeremy's mouth is open mid-sentence. Bucky's head is down at the bottom of the frame, looking like he's fixin' to contribute.

He was. Dwight says he ain't putting it in the report.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0066 — Adrian Lowe: Theft (Legion craft fair, one wreath); returned it to the wrong table
item.description: Adrian Lowe figured he could straighten out the craft fair with one wreath. At 11:20 he took it off Eli Hostetler's mother's table, two tables down from Eli's fake Amish bread, carried it to the Amish ladies' table and left it there.
item.content:encoded:
Adrian Lowe figured he could straighten out the craft fair with one wreath. At 11:20 he took it off Eli Hostetler's mother's table, two tables down from Eli's fake Amish bread, carried it to the Amish ladies' table and left it there.

"Fixing the fair," he called it. Nobody had asked him to fix a damn thing.

Twenty-two, center part tucked behind his ears, off-white tee, chin down. Stern as a man inspecting hail damage. The Amish ladies had endured Eli, Yolanda Brisbane with Sister Miriam's fur collar, and Amos hitting a boy with a pound cake right in front of them. All that bullshit, and they'd sold four loaves.

Eli's mother had thirty actual wreaths. Those ladies needed something folks would buy. Adrian said "the math was obvious." His heart was in the right place. His hands were two tables off.

"Adrian, that's not yours to move."

"Nothing's anybody's, Deputy. It's a craft fair. It's all just on tables."

Hell of a way to run retail. Stotts explained ownership. Adrian listened, chin down, giving her a fair hearing for somebody who'd just discovered property law.

Eli's mother said he could've asked. Then she said the ladies could have it anyway, walked over and gave them four more. They looked at her, then Adrian. One nodded. There now. He'd done the asking ass-backwards, but somebody understood.

He's stern in the Polaroid. Right about the math, wrong about the fair. Both are on the sheet. The wreaths sold out.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0065 — Ramon Villarreal: Disorderly conduct (football, Chicago-related)
item.description: Ramon Villarreal came from Chicago to Ponder County for a job and a girl. Then he had no job, no girl, and a lease. We kept him. At eleven he was in the Legion bar wearing a White Sox shirt among Cardinals fans, so he hadn't quit believing things could work out.
item.content:encoded:
Ramon Villarreal came from Chicago to Ponder County for a job and a girl. Then he had no job, no girl, and a lease. We kept him. At eleven he was in the Legion bar wearing a White Sox shirt among Cardinals fans, so he hadn't quit believing things could work out.

The argument was football. It's December. Wade Pettibone, booked at nine for hijacking the parade, was out by ten-thirty and back at the bar he'd hijacked it to. Wade said Chicago "hadn't done shit since Ditka."

Ramon agreed.

That was where it all went to hell. He agreed loud, at length, with the grief of a man who'd saved every receipt. Started listing seasons. Wade had come fishing for a fight and caught a whole damn funeral.

By the time Hargrove got there, half the bar was consoling Ramon. They'd have done it for any of us. Even in that shirt.

"I'm not arresting a man for being sad about the Bears."

"He's been sad for forty minutes, Deputy."

"Well, what am I supposed to put down?"

"Put down the Bears. Might help the poor son of a bitch."

Ramon's chin-up and stern in the Polaroid, earrings in, shot in the Annex. His Sox shirt is the only one in the county. It's been noted.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0064 — Leonard Ashby: Retrieving a son from a camel; interfering with an animal (Cheryl)
item.description: Derek Ashby took a camel's blanket at 10:45, got bit, laughed on the ground and got booked. That's Derek's story. His daddy's takes longer, on account of having to explain Derek.
item.content:encoded:
Derek Ashby took a camel's blanket at 10:45, got bit, laughed on the ground and got booked. That's Derek's story. His daddy's takes longer, on account of having to explain Derek.

Leonard Ashby came to the First Baptist lot at 11:15. Fifty-four, balding, mustache gray at the ends, burgundy-and-blue overshirt. Somebody'd called saying, "Derek's under a camel." By then Derek was in a cruiser. The camel had her blanket back. Leonard walked up.

"You bit my boy."

Cheryl looked at him.

"He had it coming. Hell, I'm not saying he didn't. But you bit him."

Faroukh, her owner, said, "Sir, please step back from the camel."

"I'm talking to her."

"She does not talk."

"She bit my son, she can damn well listen."

For six minutes he talked quietly to Cheryl about Derek, about Derek's mother, about how Derek was "like this at four." Cheryl didn't move. Reckon Leonard needed to tell somebody who wasn't fixin' to interrupt and say boys will be boys. Man already knew that. Had fifty-four years on him and still couldn't get ahead of this shit.

Faroukh, who's heard plenty addressed to his camel, called it "the most reasonable anyone was to her all day."

Hargrove booked Leonard for interference because Faroukh had asked twice. He's slumped and neutral in the Polaroid, unsmiling, done saying his piece. Cheryl didn't bite him. Faroukh says she wanted to. Says she chose not to. That's something.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0063 — Trina Voss: Assault (chili); disturbing a sanctioned competition
item.description: They judged the Ponder County Christmas Carnival chili cook-off at eleven, and Trina Voss didn't win. Nine years running. By now that woman could've measured disappointment with the same cup she used for beans.
item.content:encoded:
They judged the Ponder County Christmas Carnival chili cook-off at eleven, and Trina Voss didn't win. Nine years running. By now that woman could've measured disappointment with the same cup she used for beans.

Rusty Jane Walker won this year. Her own entry, 0010; look it up. Trina had come in a sleeveless top in thirty-four degrees because "you sweat over a pot." She walked her Crock-Pot to the judges' table and poured it over the head judge.

Well, shit. There went the serving suggestion.

It was good chili. Everybody said so afterward, and meant it. Wasn't first, but it didn't deserve to spend its afternoon in a man's eyebrows either.

"It's hot," the judge said, meaning temperature. Then he tasted some off his chin. "It's good."

"THEN WHY THE HELL DIDN'T IT WIN?"

Poor man had a face full of supper and no safe answer.

Sheriff Ponder walked her to the car. She went quiet. God love her, nine years is a long time to bring your best pot and carry home the same damn answer.

She's leaning forward in the Polaroid, unsmiling, red from the pot and the cold and all nine years. The judge sent a card: "Second place, if it helps."

It did not help.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0062 — Peggy Rountree "Peg": Assault (purse, Walmart layaway); smoking in a county building
item.description: Peg Rountree hit Brent Hollis with her purse in the Walmart layaway line at 6:50 a.m., posted his bail at 8:00 so he'd be out of the line, and came in at 11 to make sure he stayed out. That's follow-through. Most of us can't finish a grocery list.
item.content:encoded:
Peg Rountree hit Brent Hollis with her purse in the Walmart layaway line at 6:50 a.m., posted his bail at 8:00 so he'd be out of the line, and came in at 11 to make sure he stayed out. That's follow-through. Most of us can't finish a grocery list.

Deputy Stotts asked about the purse.

“Self-defense.”

“He said 'scuse me, Peg.”

“Seventy times. Hell, I excused him the first sixty-nine.”

While explaining, Peg lit a cigarette under the lobby's NO SMOKING sign. Dwight told her to put it out.

“In a minute.”

He took the Polaroid with it still burning. Dwight knows when to pick a fight, and a woman who has already financed the release of her own victim ain't running low on determination.

She's grinning in a big flower-basket sweatshirt, ring on her hand, smoke drifting off the top of the frame. Got to love Peg. Even getting booked, she looks pleased to see everybody.

“Is that going in the paper?”

“There's no paper, Peg. It's a Polaroid.”

“Well, shit. Take another one, then. I wasn't ready.”

He didn't. This is the one. Damn fine likeness, too.

She got a Nintendo on layaway Monday. Brent was behind her. He didn't say a word.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0061 — Kimberly Nash: Careless driving (parade route, wrong way); attempted return to Tulsa
item.description: Kimberly Nash wouldn't get out of her Cutlass. That's why this is the only Polaroid taken inside a car. Dwight couldn't fetch her a portable damn wall.
item.content:encoded:
Kimberly Nash wouldn't get out of her Cutlass. That's why this is the only Polaroid taken inside a car. Dwight couldn't fetch her a portable damn wall.

She's the Kimberly. Lindsay Fowler's Kimberly. First chair flute, Marching Wildcats, '84 to '87. Moved to Tulsa, doesn't play. Home for Thanksgiving at her mother's, meant to leave Friday, then Saturday at eight. At 11 a.m. she was still here, plaid shirt over a red tee, hair every which way, driving wrong-way down Main Street against a parade that had already ended.

Didn't know about the parade. Doesn't read the Ledger. Lives in Tulsa. Fair enough; we don't keep up with their shit either.

Reserve Deputy Toad stood in front with his hand up. She stopped. Stayed put.

"Ma'am."

"I'm just trying to get to 5."

"You're on Main."

"I KNOW I'm on Main. Where the hell else would I be stuck?"

"There was a parade."

"I don't LIVE here."

She said that four times. Toad wrote it down four times. Dear man wasn't gonna lose her side of the argument through careless paperwork.

Dwight happened to be at the Rexall buying film. Shot her through the driver's window because she wouldn't come to a wall and no wall would come to her. She's sideways in it, unsmiling.

Somebody told her later a girl named Lindsay played her old flute in the parade she'd missed.

"Lindsay Fowler? She was second chair."

She was. She's first now. Kimberly's in Tulsa.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0060 — Nicole Tremaine: Theft (one live Nativity sheep, briefly)
item.description: Nicole Tremaine, twenty-three, took a sheep. Couldn't tell you why. Asked several ways, she remained pretty firm on not knowing a damn thing about her own plan.
item.content:encoded:
Nicole Tremaine, twenty-three, took a sheep. Couldn't tell you why. Asked several ways, she remained pretty firm on not knowing a damn thing about her own plan.

Glen Whitaker's four sheep had just been unloaded at First Baptist for the Nativity. Nicole was crossing the parking lot to the craft fair in a dark hoodie. One sheep looked at her. She looked back. She opened her Escort's rear door and it climbed in.

"On its own," she said. "I ain't out here loading sheep."

No, hon. Just providing transportation.

She drove around the square twice. Said the sheep liked the radio. I believe her. Nicole wanted company, the sheep wanted a ride, and neither one had the sense to ask Glen.

Deputy Hargrove stopped her in front of the Rexall because a sheep was looking out the Escort's back window.

"Ma'am, is that a sheep?"

"It's Glen's."

"Does Glen know?"

"Glen's got three more."

"Well, hell, that's inventory. I asked about permission."

She's wide-eyed in the Polaroid, faint smile, hoodie, just discovering how little encouragement it takes to get her ass in trouble.

The sheep went back fine. Glen called it "the dumb one." Same sheep got on the highway later. Nicole says that's not her fault. It isn't. It is. You show a sheep the world, don't act surprised when the little shit wants another look.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0059 — Rusty Spurlock: Passing a bad check (to the Rusty Spur, from the Rusty Nail)
item.description: Ponder County has two bars called Rusty. The Rusty Nail's on the square and the Rusty Spur's out on the highway, and they hate each other the way two Baptist churches on the same block hate each other: quiet, polite, and till Jesus comes back.
item.content:encoded:
Ponder County has two bars called Rusty. The Rusty Nail's on the square and the Rusty Spur's out on the highway, and they hate each other the way two Baptist churches on the same block hate each other: quiet, polite, and till Jesus comes back.

Rusty Spurlock is named Rusty. He drinks at both, God love him, because a man's got to have a backup. At 10:50 Saturday morning he wrote a check at the Spur for two Bloody Marys and a pack of Winstons, and when the bartender looked at it, it was a Rusty Nail bar tab from the night before with "pay to the order of the Spur" wrote across the top and signed.

"Rusty, that ain't a goddamn check."

"It's a check the Nail owes me. I'm passin' it on."

"That is not how checks work, you jackass --"

"That's EXACTLY how checks. Money's money. Ask Preston at the bank."

Preston at the bank was in the drunk tank in a bathrobe, but Rusty didn't know that yet.

In the Polaroid he's in a navy jacket with the lining hanging out, mullet slick as owl shit, half a grin on him like a man who still believes it'll clear. Both bars have banned him, which took a summit. He drinks at the Legion now. The Legion, bless it, has a bar and no standards.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0058 — Ross Tidwell: Interference with an animal (cow); attempted milking
item.description: By 10:30 Saturday morning that cow had spent six hours loose on Highway 5. Two sale-barn men had chased it, it had stopped a donkey, and Gene Autry Pike, its officially identified owner, said he'd sold it to himself. Along came Ross Tidwell, thinking somebody ought to milk the poor damn thing.
item.content:encoded:
By 10:30 Saturday morning that cow had spent six hours loose on Highway 5. Two sale-barn men had chased it, it had stopped a donkey, and Gene Autry Pike, its officially identified owner, said he'd sold it to himself. Along came Ross Tidwell, thinking somebody ought to milk the poor damn thing.

It's a steer. Hold that thought.

Ross is thirty-eight, town-raised, red henley, hands behind his back like he's studying something valuable. Knows cattle about like most of us know airplanes: can point one out real good. He pulled over, got out with a Big Gulp cup, walked up and crouched.

God love him, he meant to help. Brought his own container and everything.

The cow watched. Been watching this county carry on all day. The Sheriff said it "had a look on it." Ross looked underneath a considerable while, then stood up.

"Marvin, I think this cow's broke."

"It's a steer, Ross."

"It's a what?"

"It's a boy."

Well, shit. Ross looked at the cow. Cow looked at Ross. Whatever passed between them wouldn't fill that cup.

Booked for interference, mostly because the Sheriff had to say something. Ross is serious in the Polaroid, head tilted, hands back, still trying to get the livestock straight in his head. Everybody's called it the cow all day. Everybody's gonna keep calling it the cow. Ross would like it noted that he was the only one who checked what the hell was under it.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0057 — Derek Ashby: Stealing (one camel blanket); cruelty to animals, dismissed
item.description: At 10:30 a camel arrived at First Baptist in a trailer from Lebanon, Missouri. Faroukh, the man who brought her, doesn't do Nativities. He does "appearances." Reckon that distinction matters come tax time. The camel was Cheryl. She came with a blanket.
item.content:encoded:
At 10:30 a camel arrived at First Baptist in a trailer from Lebanon, Missouri. Faroukh, the man who brought her, doesn't do Nativities. He does "appearances." Reckon that distinction matters come tax time. The camel was Cheryl. She came with a blanket.

Derek Ashby was twenty-six, black shirt, cardigan, teeth like a game show, standing in the parking lot for reasons he couldn't later supply. He saw the blanket. Nice blanket. Took it right off Cheryl, in front of Cheryl, which left precious little room for bullshit about who'd done it.

Cheryl bit him.

Deputy Hargrove came to sort out the donkey situation and found Derek on the ground under a camel, laughing too hard to get up. Still had the blanket in his fist. Boy'd surrendered most everything but his grip.

"Why the hell'd you take it?"

"It was on a camel!"

That was the whole defense. Same damn fact the prosecution was fixin' to use, only happier.

God love him, Derek knew a story worth telling when it had hold of him. Smiled all through booking. He's smiling in the Polaroid like a man who got bit by a camel in Missouri and appreciates the gift. You can't order that shit out of a catalog.

The cruelty charge was dropped. Cheryl was fine. She got her blanket back and kept the piece of Derek.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0056 — Annette Purcell: Shoplifting (one Polaroid camera, Rexall); returned, used
item.description: The booking camera died Thanksgiving night. Dwight used his own Polaroid till ten Saturday morning, when the film ran out. Annette Purcell heard through her sister Wanda, the Avon lady, over breakfast. Around here news gets delivered with the biscuits whether you ordered any or not.
item.content:encoded:
The booking camera died Thanksgiving night. Dwight used his own Polaroid till ten Saturday morning, when the film ran out. Annette Purcell heard through her sister Wanda, the Avon lady, over breakfast. Around here news gets delivered with the biscuits whether you ordered any or not.

Annette went to the Rexall. Didn't buy film. Took a whole Spectra off the shelf, the good camera, plus four packs, and walked out in her burgundy coat with the yellow lining.

Drove straight to jail and handed it to Dwight. “Here.”

“Annette, did you pay for this?”

“It's for the county.”

“The county's got to pay for it, then.”

“Well, the county can arrest my ass and use the camera to do it.”

Which it did. That's public service with the paperwork attached.

This is the first Polaroid off the stolen Spectra. She's smiling, head tilted, hunched and pleased as punch. Damn right. A hundred more people were coming, and Annette was the only reason any of them got a picture. Woman saw a need and filled it. Skipped a register, but filled it.

The Rexall sent a bill. The Sheriff paid out of the coffee fund. Hell, it was fine. Nobody drinks that coffee. You could warsh a tractor part in it and make the part worse.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0055 — Crystal Vanderpool: Solicitation of a peace officer (romantic); interference
item.description: Crystal Vanderpool came to the Sheriff's Office at 10:20 a.m. to bail out her brother Dallas, the fake Shriner. Didn't commit a crime. Still left a booking Polaroid behind. Woman knew what she wanted and wasn't about to let the absence of wrongdoing gum it up.
item.content:encoded:
Crystal Vanderpool came to the Sheriff's Office at 10:20 a.m. to bail out her brother Dallas, the fake Shriner. Didn't commit a crime. Still left a booking Polaroid behind. Woman knew what she wanted and wasn't about to let the absence of wrongdoing gum it up.

"Marvin," she told Sheriff Ponder, "you've been a widower six years. I've been divorced two. It's December. Take a picture of me for your desk."

Marvin said that wasn't what the camera was for.

"Then arrest me, damn it."

"For what?"

She considered that in her burgundy paisley top, all that hair waiting on an answer. "Loitering with intent."

He wrote it down. Crossed it out. Poor dear man could handle a jail full of drunks, but a woman volunteering to like him had his pen plumb confused.

Dwight knew when to quit watching a decent man wrestle his own ass. He took the picture anyway, out in the hall in front of the door marked SHERIFF. Crystal tilted her head like she'd had this planned since Thanksgiving. She had. Dallas getting arrested was about the only part she hadn't needed to arrange.

There's no charge on file. The Polaroid's on Marvin's desk. He'll tell you it's evidence, and we let him. Hell, it's evidence somebody's sweet on him. Ain't nobody disputing that.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0054 — Bernard Kaplan: Practicing law without a license (actual lawyer, wrong state)
item.description: Sherry Lindquist started bond hearings at the fingerprint shelf at 9:45. She does taxes. Somebody had to. At 10:25 Bernard Kaplan walked into the lobby in a charcoal blazer, big glasses and a beard, and watched five minutes of shit he hadn't covered in law school.
item.content:encoded:
Sherry Lindquist started bond hearings at the fingerprint shelf at 9:45. She does taxes. Somebody had to. At 10:25 Bernard Kaplan walked into the lobby in a charcoal blazer, big glasses and a beard, and watched five minutes of shit he hadn't covered in law school.

"I'm sorry, is this a court?"

Actual attorney. Champaign, Illinois. Driving to Branson with his wife for a show. They'd stopped for gas, she'd gone to the Rexall, and he'd wandered across the square because he likes courthouses. Bless him, some men look at bass boats. Bernard found a tax preparer releasing prisoners.

"Ma'am, you can't set bail."

"Who are you?"

"I'm a lawyer."

"Where?"

"Illinois."

"Then you can't either, honey."

Bernard explained principle. Sherry explained how many people were still back yonder. Dale Bailey collected on two more while they argued. The Sheriff came out at 10:30 on a Saturday to find out what the hell needed this much explaining.

"Sir, are you licensed in Missouri?"

"No, but—"

"Then you're doing what she's doing."

Well, damn. Hard to rescue the law when the law's fixin' to put you beside it.

They booked him. In the Polaroid his mouth's a little open; he's still got some sentence left. His wife came back with Tums and found him in a cell with Louella. They made the show, barely. Bernard says he'll never look at a courthouse again. He will.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0053 — Casey Lindgren: Unlawful sale of raffle tickets (for a raffle that does not exist)
item.description: Casey Lindgren sold two hundred and six raffle tickets at the Legion craft fair between nine and ten-fifteen. Dollar apiece for a chance at “the quilt.” Fine offer. Small hitch: there wasn't a damn quilt.
item.content:encoded:
Casey Lindgren sold two hundred and six raffle tickets at the Legion craft fair between nine and ten-fifteen. Dollar apiece for a chance at “the quilt.” Fine offer. Small hitch: there wasn't a damn quilt.

There was the Baptist ladies' quilt table. Casey stood close enough, cream top and big honest smile, that people assumed. Casey assumed right along with them. Most businesses would charge extra for that kind of confidence.

Deputy Hargrove asked which quilt.

“One of those. I hadn't picked.”

“You were gonna buy a quilt with the raffle money and raffle it.”

“Yes.”

“Casey, that's just selling a quilt for two hundred dollars.”

“With SUSPENSE.”

Hell, put it that way and the whole craft fair sounds underambitious. The Baptist ladies hadn't known they were the prize. Once told, they weren't entirely against it. They'd been trying to move that log-cabin pattern since Easter; by now they'd have considered shooting it out of a cannon.

God love Casey, that smile could get a mule interested in financing. It's in the Polaroid, leaning in, eyes a little left toward somebody who might yet buy a ticket. Arrest ain't closed the booth.

For all the bullshit required to get there, the drawing was held at four. Louella Fenwick won. She's using it in the cell.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0052 — Hailey Pruitt: None (minor); photographed at her own request; kept the time
item.description: Hailey Pruitt came in at ten Saturday morning with Owen and the sandwich, and before long she'd found what was wrong with the whole operation. She's twelve. Dwight's daughter, Owen's sister. While Owen gave the jail art direction, she stood under the clock.
item.content:encoded:
Hailey Pruitt came in at ten Saturday morning with Owen and the sandwich, and before long she'd found what was wrong with the whole operation. She's twelve. Dwight's daughter, Owen's sister. While Owen gave the jail art direction, she stood under the clock.

It says BULOVA and CLINTON, MO. Been wrong since the power quit in August. One calendar said October 1994, the other January 1995. Hailey, black shirt with a red thing on it, looked around at all this assistance.

"Dad, nothing in here knows what time it is."

"I know it."

"Then how do you write down when people came in?"

Off his watch, naturally. Watch was slow. Dwight didn't know yet. Hailey did; she'd checked against the Rexall's. You can raise a child yourself and still get caught unprepared when she turns out competent.

So she kept time all day. Stool under the wrong clock, notebook ready. Every time Dwight shot somebody, she called the real time and he wrote it down. Didn't argue with her, either. Man knew good help when it stood under his clock in a black shirt.

Every time on every Polaroid from 10:15 a.m. on is Hailey's. Everything before is wrong by eleven minutes. Ain't anybody fixed those.

He shot her at 10:15 because she asked. No charge. Pursed lips, level look, under the clock. She wrote her own time on it. Only one in the pile she's sure of. She checked.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0051 — Eli Hostetler: Selling without a permit; misrepresentation of a baked good
item.description: Eli Hostetler was nineteen and selling friendship by the loaf at the Legion craft fair. His sign said "Amish Friendship Bread, $4." Eli ain't Amish. The goods weren't bread. Sara Lee pound cake, box thrown away, dishtowel pulled over the evidence. Four dollars for cake and a little bullshit.
item.content:encoded:
Eli Hostetler was nineteen and selling friendship by the loaf at the Legion craft fair. His sign said "Amish Friendship Bread, $4." Eli ain't Amish. The goods weren't bread. Sara Lee pound cake, box thrown away, dishtowel pulled over the evidence. Four dollars for cake and a little bullshit.

By ten he'd sold thirty-one loaves. The Amish ladies next door, selling actual bread they had actually made, had sold four. Well, hell. You can see where that'd take some of the pleasure out of kneading.

They didn't complain. Those ladies don't. They looked at Eli till he felt it, then looked at the Sheriff till he felt responsible for it. No raised voices. Just passed the trouble down the table like a bowl of beans.

"It's got friendship in it," Eli said. "I was friendly."

"Son, it's got a UPC on the bottom."

"Didn't charge extra for that."

God love the boy. Cornered, and still trying to give somebody a bargain. The Sheriff had to admire the nerve, even if the damn dishtowel wasn't much of a business license.

In the Polaroid Eli stands straight in his pink-striped shirt. That's the face of a boy figuring his mother will hear about this shit before he gets home. She did. She was two tables down, selling wreaths.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0050 — Vicki Sandoval: Assault (on a Shriner); interference with a parade
item.description: At 9:40 a.m., Vicki Sandoval stood outside the Rexall with her two kids when a Shriner go-kart clipped her stroller. Not Dallas Yancey this time. An actual Shriner, a dentist named Phil.
item.content:encoded:
At 9:40 a.m., Vicki Sandoval stood outside the Rexall with her two kids when a Shriner go-kart clipped her stroller. Not Dallas Yancey this time. An actual Shriner, a dentist named Phil.

The stroller was empty. Phil considered that the key fact. Vicki figured Phil was fixin' to learn something.

She chased him a block and a half in a black T-shirt with the sleeves cut off and caught him. Parade go-karts do eight miles an hour. Vicki, forty-six and madder than a wet hen, does whatever the hell is required. She pulled him out by the fez.

"It was EMPTY!" Phil said.

"It's the PRINCIPLE, you tasseled son of a bitch."

Hard to present a second argument while a woman has hold of your parade hat. Poor Phil. A man can know every tooth in your head and still misjudge your mother.

Reserve Deputy Toad had already been hit by a go-kart that morning. He took his sweet time arriving. Said it was his leg. Sure, honey. That leg had opinions.

Vicki's dead serious in the Polaroid, taken at the Legion Annex against a March 1995 calendar. Closest to right anybody got all damn day. Can't fault a mama for wanting wheels kept off her babies' things.

Phil's fine. His fez isn't. The kids thought it was the best parade ever.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0049 — Chad Ferrell: Assault (snowball, packed); disturbing the peace
item.description: It has not snowed in Ponder County. Get that straight before Chad Ferrell starts explaining. At 9:50 a.m. he threw a snowball off the Rexall roof at the Grand Marshal's Cadillac and broke the windshield. Clear weather. Frozen damn precipitation coming down from the drugstore.
item.content:encoded:
It has not snowed in Ponder County. Get that straight before Chad Ferrell starts explaining. At 9:50 a.m. he threw a snowball off the Rexall roof at the Grand Marshal's Cadillac and broke the windshield. Clear weather. Frozen damn precipitation coming down from the drugstore.

Chad, wearing a black shirt with a baseball on it, wanted credit for planning ahead. He'd made the snowball Wednesday during the flurries and kept it in his mom's deep freeze "for the parade." Three days. Rock in the middle "for structure."

Around here we generally call that a rock, but bless his heart, Chad had put work into the outside.

"It was a plan," he said.

Sure as shit was. That's the troubling part. An accident you might could talk a boy out of repeating.

The Grand Marshal was Mike Keith, of Mike Keith Insurance. His calendars hang on every wall in the jail. Turns out the man is real well insured, which is a hell of a thing to have demonstrated during your parade.

Reserve Deputy Toad, still shaky from the go-kart, stood under the ladder. "I can wait." No climbing after him. Toad had already had enough transportation bullshit.

Chad looks serious against the height chart in the Polaroid. Five-ten. The snowball was recovered. It's in the evidence freezer with the turkey. Reckon they can discuss structure.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0048 — Lindsay Fowler: Interference with a parade (band); took a flute
item.description: Everybody blamed Norma June Wiley for the flute. Miss Twirl 1973, her own entry, 0003, was passed out in the high school trophy case Saturday morning holding a baton. Seemed a fair place to start, but hell, a woman can't steal everything.
item.content:encoded:
Everybody blamed Norma June Wiley for the flute. Miss Twirl 1973, her own entry, 0003, was passed out in the high school trophy case Saturday morning holding a baton. Seemed a fair place to start, but hell, a woman can't steal everything.

It was Lindsay Fowler. Twenty-six, Marching Wildcats flute section from '84 to '87, second chair behind Kimberly, who lives in Tulsa now and doesn't even play. That last part still chaps Lindsay's ass.

Friday night, while Norma June was carrying on, Lindsay took a school flute from the band room. They'd sold her old one. Saturday at 9:45 she stepped into the Main Street parade beside the flute section, cream T-shirt, blue scrunchie, and went right to playing.

"Joy to the World." She knew every damn note. Fifteen-year-olds on either side kept looking over like the school had started holding folks back eight years.

The band director admitted she was "first chair, honestly." God love her, she'd finally moved up by aging out.

Hargrove pulled her out at Oak Street.

"Lindsay, you're not in the band."

"I was."

"Eight years ago."

"Well, shit, I still know it."

She's subdued in the Polaroid, shoulders rounded in a dark corner, red sign behind her. The flute's in evidence beside the tuba Tyler Nance took. The band director says she can sit in at the spring concert. Lindsay said she'd think about it. She's thinking about it.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0047 — Sherry Lindquist: Practicing law without a license (bond hearing, unofficial)
item.description: By 9:30 a.m. the Ponder County jail had twenty-eight people in fourteen beds, and Judge Renfro was somewhere up a tree with his radio off. Deer stand. Important distinction if you're the judge; didn't mean shit to anybody needing bail.
item.content:encoded:
By 9:30 a.m. the Ponder County jail had twenty-eight people in fourteen beds, and Judge Renfro was somewhere up a tree with his radio off. Deer stand. Important distinction if you're the judge; didn't mean shit to anybody needing bail.

In walked Sherry Lindquist, who does taxes. She sat at the fingerprint shelf beside Dale "Bail" Bailey, opened a legal pad, and started holding bond hearings. No fuss. Woman saw paperwork needing done.

She called names. Folks stood. What'd you do, and were you sorry? Fifty dollars for sorry, a hundred for not, twenty-five for Louella Fenwick because "honey, no." Hell, at least you could understand the rates.

She'd heard nine and Dale had collected on six before Dwight asked who she was.

"I'm the judge."

"You do my taxes, Sherry."

"Then you know I'm thorough."

That was a damn awkward credential to argue with. Dwight trusted her with deductions he couldn't pronounce. God love her, she'd come to a room full of trouble and found something useful to do with a pen.

In the Polaroid she's beaming in her striped blouse, standing by the office door like she owns the place. For forty minutes she did. Nobody she released came back. The real judge got in Monday and honored all nine.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0046 — Nate Corrigan: Careless driving (Shriner go-kart, borrowed); parade interference
item.description: Dallas Yancey lined his own go-kart up with the Shriners at 8:15, got run out, and ran over Toad. Phil the dentist clipped a stroller and got pulled out by the fez. At 9:30, with the Shriners regrouping behind the Rexall, Phil's commotion drew one Shriner away from a running kart.
item.content:encoded:
Dallas Yancey lined his own go-kart up with the Shriners at 8:15, got run out, and ran over Toad. Phil the dentist clipped a stroller and got pulled out by the fez. At 9:30, with the Shriners regrouping behind the Rexall, Phil's commotion drew one Shriner away from a running kart.

Nate Corrigan got in. Thirty-one, not a Shriner, sunglasses hanging from his shirt's V. Serious face. Nate generally doesn't do things. By God, he was fixin' to do one.

He drove one block in the parade behind the band. Shriner speed: eight miles an hour. Looks like nothing from the curb; down there by the pavement, I reckon it felt like hauling ass. No waving, no figure-eights. Straight behind the tubas, hands at ten and two, sunglasses swinging. Most responsible damn theft of a ride you've ever seen.

At Church Street he pulled over, climbed out, and stood beside it. Toad, still shaky, looked him over.

“You're not a Shriner.”

“No.”

“Then why—”

“I've always wanted to.”

Well, hell. Toad understood. Everybody does. A little kart, a block of music, a thing you finally got to do. He booked Nate anyway.

Nate's serious in the Polaroid, sunglasses still there. He'll never do anything like that again and doesn't need to. The Shriner got his kart back. Said it was “warm.”

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0045 — Nathan Coble: Impersonating Santa Claus (understudy); tractor theft
item.description: Nathan Coble saw a running tractor and a Santa float without a Santa, and figured somebody ought to do something. Nathan is twenty-two, striped shirt, face like a Sunday. Give that boy half a chance to help and he'll help your ass clean into a charge.
item.content:encoded:
Nathan Coble saw a running tractor and a Santa float without a Santa, and figured somebody ought to do something. Nathan is twenty-two, striped shirt, face like a Sunday. Give that boy half a chance to help and he'll help your ass clean into a charge.

The parade had stalled at the Legion. Santa went inside for "one beer," leaving the tractor running and his suit on the seat because the Legion runs hot. Kids waited on the sidewalk. Nathan didn't see a theft. He saw folks fixing to be disappointed.

He put on the suit and drove four blocks down Main to the Pentecostal church, the one Wade Pettibone had rerouted the whole parade around. Idled there twenty minutes, waving and ho ho ho-ing in a voice he later admitted "was mostly Cody Whitlow's dad."

The Pentecostals clapped. Wade was wrong as hell about that.

Real Santa reported the tractor stolen at 9:25. Deputy Hargrove found Nathan passing out candy canes he'd discovered in the float's glove box.

"Step down, Nathan."

"One more block?"

Hargrove gave him one. Damn decent of him, considering he'd have to explain why a stolen tractor got an extension.

In the Polaroid Nathan's still got that little smile. Ain't a lick of bullshit in it. He knows what he did.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0044 — Patsy Delacroix: Disturbing a lawful assembly; assault on a game show host (effigy)
item.description: Patsy Delacroix has watched The Price Is Right every weekday since 1974 and has never been wrong about a showcase. Argue if you want. I'd sooner kick a wasp nest in my church shoes.
item.content:encoded:
Patsy Delacroix has watched The Price Is Right every weekday since 1974 and has never been wrong about a showcase. Argue if you want. I'd sooner kick a wasp nest in my church shoes.

The Legion craft fair opened at nine, in the same hall where the parade had just crashed to a halt. The Methodist men's group had made a life-size plywood Bob Barker for a photo booth. Fifty cents a picture. Patsy paid. Looked at him a good long while.

Wrong hair color. Wrong microphone shape. She told the men they ought to be ashamed of that damn thing, and they laughed. Well, shit. You don't laugh during an inspection.

She knocked his head off with her pocketbook.

“That is not Bob,” she told the Sheriff from a folding chair, red-striped blouse and pink bow, dressed nice for a day nobody had managed to deserve. “You don't get to make a Bob. Especially not that sorry-ass Bob.”

Bless her heart, she'd paid for a picture with somebody she'd eaten lunch with for twenty-one years. They'd handed her lumber with a haircut.

Dwight shot her right there under the BOB BARKER sign, head hanging, jaw set. Come on down. Mind the head.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0043 — Wade Pettibone: Contributing to the delinquency of a minor; parade interference (father)
item.description: Wade Pettibone and his boy Junior got booked together at 9 a.m. and photographed together because Dwight was out of wall. Not film. Wall. That's the kind of Saturday we were having.
item.content:encoded:
Wade Pettibone and his boy Junior got booked together at 9 a.m. and photographed together because Dwight was out of wall. Not film. Wall. That's the kind of Saturday we were having.

Wade is Booster Club clear to the bone. His shirt says CLUB beneath a wildcat that looks like it lost an argument with a grain truck. Arms folded, he told Deputy Hargrove the Christmas parade ought not pass the Pentecostal church because “they don't clap.”

“Band works hard. Least folks could move their damn hands.”

So at 8:50, when the band turned onto Church Street, Wade and Junior blocked the intersection with Wade's Silverado and stood in the bed holding THIS WAY, pointed toward the Legion.

The band followed. They're fifteen-year-olds; give them a sign and they'll follow it plumb into next week. The Shriners followed the band. Santa's tractor followed the Shriners. Whole parade fetched up at the Legion Hall and stopped, because the Legion has a bar. Hell of a navigation aid, a bar.

“Best turnout we ever had,” Wade said.

Can't fault the man's affection for a school band. His judgment's another sack of shit entirely.

Junior smiled for the Polaroid. Wade didn't. Wade knows the routine. Junior's learning it, and apparently driver education comes with matching shirts.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0042 — Josh Wexler: Truancy (Saturday); trespass on school property
item.description: Josh Wexler got picked up for truancy on a Saturday. The Sheriff admitted that was "not a thing," but wrote it down because Josh asked him to. Around here we might could arrest you for something that ain't possible, if you ask decent.
item.content:encoded:
Josh Wexler got picked up for truancy on a Saturday. The Sheriff admitted that was "not a thing," but wrote it down because Josh asked him to. Around here we might could arrest you for something that ain't possible, if you ask decent.

Josh is sixteen, Nike shirt, cap with the green underside showing, face still waiting to see how things turn out. At 8:30 a.m. he was in the high school band room, sitting in the tuba chair and playing nothing. Tyler Nance had the tuba. Tyler was in jail. Whole damn instrument section gone before breakfast.

"I just wanted to see what it felt like," Josh said.

"The chair?"

"Yeah."

Sheriff Ponder had come about the raccoons. He sat in the trombone chair, and neither said anything awhile. Good man. He could spare a kid some quiet; the raccoons could keep tearing up whatever the hell they were tearing up.

Then he said, "Well, you're trespassing."

"Can I be truant instead? It sounds better."

The Sheriff said sure. Trespassing sounds like you're up to some shit. Truant at least suggests somebody expected you.

In the Polaroid Josh has one arm across the frame and his mouth a little open, like he's still in that chair. His mom bailed him out at 9:10, in time to watch the parade go by without a tuba in it.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0041 — Curtis Blevins: Property damage (paint); vandalism of a municipal water tower, attempted
item.description: Before Adam "Double Adam" McCoy set the water tower on fire that night, Curtis Blevins tried to paint it. Adam's got his own entry. One municipal improvement at a time, for hell's sake.
item.content:encoded:
Before Adam "Double Adam" McCoy set the water tower on fire that night, Curtis Blevins tried to paint it. Adam's got his own entry. One municipal improvement at a time, for hell's sake.

Curtis climbed up at dawn with two gallons of white and a roller on a broom handle. He meant to cover PONDER COUNTY and write “something true.” Hadn't settled on what. He was gonna “let the tower tell him.”

Bless his heart, most of us can't get an answer out of the county at ground level.

The tower didn't say shit. The wind, however, had considerable input.

At 8:20 a.m. Deputy Hargrove found Curtis back on the ground, roller in hand, covered head to foot in his own paint. His pink T-shirt had been red an hour earlier. The tower was untouched except for one word he'd managed before the wind turned, eight feet tall: THE.

“THE what, Curtis?”

“I was getting to it.”

“Whole damn town's on the edge of its seat.”

Curtis's eyes are nearly closed in the Polaroid, speckled like a bird's egg. You want to laugh, but the man did climb a water tower for the truth. We mostly just holler for it from a stool.

The THE was still there when the fire started.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0040 — Dallas Yancey: Disorderly conduct; unauthorized Shriner
item.description: Dallas Yancey is twenty, ain't a Shriner, and does not own a fez. He does own a go-kart. At 8 a.m. on parade day he lined up with the Shriners' go-karts in a red puffy coat and purple shirt, figuring the rest might sort itself out.
item.content:encoded:
Dallas Yancey is twenty, ain't a Shriner, and does not own a fez. He does own a go-kart. At 8 a.m. on parade day he lined up with the Shriners' go-karts in a red puffy coat and purple shirt, figuring the rest might sort itself out.

That's a hell of a lot to ask of a puffy coat.

The Shriners looked closely. When the Grand Potentate asked to see his fez, Dallas said it was "in the shop." Asked which shop, he did a lap. Then several more. Boy was trying to outrun a follow-up question at lawnmower speed.

Reserve Deputy Toad stepped in front of the kart with his hand up. Toad directs parade traffic once a year and got deputized by accident in 1988. He trusted that hand more than was sensible.

"Whoa, damn it!"

Toad's fine. He's just slow now. Dallas hadn't meant to hurt a soul; he wanted in the parade so bad he'd forgotten somebody might be standing in it.

In the Polaroid he's hunched and serious under the NO SMOKING sign, the only one all day who looked like he felt bad. He did. Felt like shit, poor kid. Wrote Toad a letter, too. Toad framed it. It's in the hallway.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0039 — Wesley Grimm "Nature Boy": Unlawful release of wildlife (parade); possession of eleven raccoons
item.description: Wesley Grimm called his float “Missouri's Bounty.” Flatbed, hay bales, eleven raccoons in a wire pen. He'd been live-trapping since Halloween. Most folks would've stopped at one raccoon and asked what the hell they were doing.
item.content:encoded:
Wesley Grimm called his float “Missouri's Bounty.” Flatbed, hay bales, eleven raccoons in a wire pen. He'd been live-trapping since Halloween. Most folks would've stopped at one raccoon and asked what the hell they were doing.

The Jaycees told him no Thursday. Wesley showed up anyway in a T-shirt with eagles and a canyon, smiling that little smile of a man who figures permission is mostly for indoor things. God love him, he'd brought the whole damn outdoors.

At 7:55 the Shriners' go-karts fired up behind him in the staging lot. Raccoons don't care for go-karts. Turns out they didn't care for his pen, either.

By the time Deputy Hargrove got the cuffs on, there were raccoons in the Baptist float's manger, in the Sonic Drive-In float's fake tater tots, and on the Jaycees' truck roof. One was inside the tuba Tyler Nance had just been arrested for. That son of a bitch had found the only parade seat with a bell on it.

“They're bounty,” Wesley said. “They'll come back.”

Nine did. Pretty fair return on a wildlife investment, considering the shit he'd put them through.

The calendar behind him in the Polaroid says September 1994. Nothing in this building is current.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0038 — Tyler Nance: Stealing under $150 (one tuba)
item.description: Tyler Nance, fifteen, plays trombone in the Ponder County High School Marching Wildcats. He's wanted the tuba since he was nine, when somebody told him his arms were too short. His arms caught up. The tuba chair didn't. Six years is a hell of a wait for permission to go oom-pah.
item.content:encoded:
Tyler Nance, fifteen, plays trombone in the Ponder County High School Marching Wildcats. He's wanted the tuba since he was nine, when somebody told him his arms were too short. His arms caught up. The tuba chair didn't. Six years is a hell of a wait for permission to go oom-pah.

At 7:30 a.m., ninety minutes before the Christmas parade, Tyler took the tuba.

Didn't hide it. Walked down Main Street carrying the damn thing, which is about as sneaky as stealing a grain bin. He meant to march. That was the whole plan, clear to the fence line.

Deputy Hargrove called it “the most honest thing I saw all day.” Hard to dispute a boy advertising his theft in brass.

In the Polaroid Tyler's grinning, striped button-up on, like he'd ordered this exact Saturday. Behind him is a MIKE KEITH INSURANCE calendar saying November 1994. Nobody in that building flips shit except occasionally their lid.

The band director declined to press charges. Also declined to let him march. Fair enough, but you hate to see a dream get parked indoors.

Tyler played the tuba in the holding cell for an hour. Every note was wrong. Dwight says it was beautiful, and I reckon a man that tired knows joy when it rattles the plumbing.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0037 — Gene Autry Pike "Gene Autry": Animal at large; failure to control livestock (the cow)
item.description: That cow loose on Highway 5 all of December 2, 1995 belonged, on paper, to Gene Autry Pike. Same cow that stopped the donkey, ate the Nativity hay, and walked into the sale barn at midnight like it had called ahead. Busy damn cow.
item.content:encoded:
That cow loose on Highway 5 all of December 2, 1995 belonged, on paper, to Gene Autry Pike. Same cow that stopped the donkey, ate the Nativity hay, and walked into the sale barn at midnight like it had called ahead. Busy damn cow.

Gene Autry said he didn't have one.

Black jacket with racing stripes, cap, head down, half a smile. You know that smile. That's a man whose wife already heard this bullshit and didn't buy any.

"Then whose brand is on it, Gene?"

"Mine. But I sold that cow."

"To who?"

"Myself. Different year."

Now, I like Gene. Most everybody does. But he'd argue with a fencepost and then send the fencepost a bill for standing there.

Sheriff Ponder booked him at seven. Wasn't gonna help a lick, but four calls had come in and the Sheriff needed a name to put on the cow. The cow wasn't offering one. Hell, the cow had places to be.

In the Polaroid there's a fellow asleep at a table behind him. That's Lonnie. He's still there. Between Lonnie and Gene, you had two men available and neither taking responsibility for a hoof.

The cow was never booked. The cow had a better day than anybody.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0036 — Brent Hollis: Theft of services (Walmart layaway line)
item.description: Brent Hollis was seventy-first in the Walmart layaway line at 6:15 a.m. and first at 6:50. Nobody could say exactly how. You'd have thought a man wearing a blue plaid shirt over two other shirts would've been easier to track.
item.content:encoded:
Brent Hollis was seventy-first in the Walmart layaway line at 6:15 a.m. and first at 6:50. Nobody could say exactly how. You'd have thought a man wearing a blue plaid shirt over two other shirts would've been easier to track.

He inched along saying, "'scuse me, my wife's up here," seventy times. Slow. Apologetic. Polite as a church usher moving you away from the good fan.

Brent ain't got a wife. He's got a Super Nintendo on layaway and a nephew he's already told. That's a hell of a promise to make a little boy, and God love him, he meant to keep it. His methods were shit.

The line caught on at the counter. A Missouri line in December has cold feet and a damn good memory. Peg hit him with her purse. A man held his collar till Deputy Stotts arrived, Brent still saying "'scuse me," apparently hoping manners might could reverse a felony.

In the Polaroid he's leaning back, looking serious off to the left, like that whole line's still behind him.

It is. Peg posted his bail so she could stand in front of him again Monday. Woman wasn't finished waiting.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0035 — Kyle Mattingly: Careless driving; failure to secure a load (one Nativity donkey)
item.description: First Baptist rented a donkey for the live Nativity off a man in Lebanon, and Kyle Mattingly got sent to fetch it in his Ranger at 5 a.m., because Kyle is the youth pastor's brother-in-law and that, friends, is how church works.
item.content:encoded:
First Baptist rented a donkey for the live Nativity off a man in Lebanon, and Kyle Mattingly got sent to fetch it in his Ranger at 5 a.m., because Kyle is the youth pastor's brother-in-law and that, friends, is how church works.

Kyle did not bring a trailer. Kyle put a donkey in the bed of a Ford Ranger with a tarp over it and one bungee cord across, and that donkey rode standing up at fifty-five down Highway 5 with its head over the cab like a hood ornament straight out of hell.

The donkey was fine. The donkey, by every account, was having the time of its damn life.

Deputy Hargrove pulled him over at the sale barn, where the loose cow was standing square in the road like it owned the county, and the donkey and the cow looked at each other a good long while, the way two old boys do at a funeral when they ain't sure if they're kin.

"Jesus Christ, Kyle."

"He wanted to see out."

"He's a DONKEY."

"Well, he sure as shit didn't want to see IN."

Kyle's squinting in the Polaroid, blue tee and cap, like a man trying to work out what the charge for a donkey even is. Failure to secure a load. The donkey made the Nativity. Nobody asked how it got there. The cow watched Kyle go, and Hargrove swears it shook its head.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0034 — Randy Culpepper "Sunshine": Public indecency (tanning); operating a tanning bed without a license
item.description: Randy Culpepper bought a tanning bed off a salon in Osage Beach that went under. No salon of his own, no room big enough at the house, so he set it in a horse trailer behind Sunset Lanes and ran an extension cord into the bowling alley's wall. Well, hell. Electricity don't care whether you've got a reception desk.
item.content:encoded:
Randy Culpepper bought a tanning bed off a salon in Osage Beach that went under. No salon of his own, no room big enough at the house, so he set it in a horse trailer behind Sunset Lanes and ran an extension cord into the bowling alley's wall. Well, hell. Electricity don't care whether you've got a reception desk.

He's his own best customer. Look at those shoulders. That ain't a tan you get piddlin' around with yard work.

At 6:10 a.m. Deputy Stotts answered a call about "a blue light and a man's voice going 'ohhh' behind the lanes." She opened the trailer. Randy wore a tank top, a cap, a gold chain, and nothing you'd call pants. Eyes shut. Smiling like the light bill was somebody else's.

"It's for the dance tonight. You can't show up to the VFW pale."

"Randy, it's a horse trailer."

"Horses don't need it. They're outside."

"Your ass is inside, and I can see it from outside."

He didn't let that spoil a damn thing. God love him, all he wanted was to look nice at the dance. Some men buy a shirt; Randy cooks the parts that stick out.

He rode in without opening his eyes. In the Polaroid he still hasn't. Happiest man in the building, no bullshit about it. And he's orange.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0033 — Kayla Sprouse "Miss Ponder County 1995": Theft (one parade float, partial)
item.description: Kayla Sprouse, Miss Ponder County 1995, learned Friday she'd be sharing this year's parade float with Miss Ponder County 1994. That'd be her cousin Brandi. They hadn't spoken since the Fourth of July over a jet ski, and apparently a whole damn float wasn't enough room to continue not speaking.
item.content:encoded:
Kayla Sprouse, Miss Ponder County 1995, learned Friday she'd be sharing this year's parade float with Miss Ponder County 1994. That'd be her cousin Brandi. They hadn't spoken since the Fourth of July over a jet ski, and apparently a whole damn float wasn't enough room to continue not speaking.

At 5:45 a.m. Deputy Hargrove found Kayla in the fairgrounds equipment barn, taking a Sawzall to the float. She'd done the math. Her half had the throne. Brandi's half had opportunities.

Floral blouse, bow off her sash, calm as you please. Most folks look caught when a deputy walks in. Kayla looked like he'd come to help load.

"It's technically my float. The Jaycees gave it to me. I'm giving Brandi some of it."

"You're giving her the trailer hitch, Kayla."

"She can pull."

"How the hell am I supposed to write this up?"

"Put down sharing."

You had to love her nerve. We'd crowned her for poise, and by God, she was keeping her ass poised through a theft investigation.

In the Polaroid she's leaning back, half-lidded, hands folded in her lap, waiting on judges she reckons she can win over. Made bail by 8:30 and rode at nine. Sure as shit, Brandi walked behind carrying the hitch.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0032 — Lonnie Baskett: Sleeping in a public place (Lions Club pancake breakfast, pre-opening)
item.description: The Lions Club found Lonnie Baskett asleep under the griddle at 5:20 a.m. inside the fire station. Padded jacket over a Flintstones T-shirt. Bottle of syrup already open. That boy wasn't leaving a damn thing to chance except waking up.
item.content:encoded:
The Lions Club found Lonnie Baskett asleep under the griddle at 5:20 a.m. inside the fire station. Padded jacket over a Flintstones T-shirt. Bottle of syrup already open. That boy wasn't leaving a damn thing to chance except waking up.

He hadn't broken in. He'd attended the Friday-night fish fry, eaten, and stayed put. The firemen figured he was a Lion. The Lions figured he was a fireman. Everybody turned out the lights. Hell, between two civic organizations you'd think somebody could identify a man full of fish.

"I was first in line," Lonnie told Sheriff Ponder, eyes still shut.

"Lonnie, the line starts outside."

"That's a policy, not a law."

Had him there. Sheriff came for pancakes himself, not a constitutional argument from underneath the cooking equipment.

The Lions were carrying on, so he wrote Lonnie up mostly to hush them, then let him eat first. Decent man. No sense making somebody's breakfast cold just because his ass got there too early.

Lonnie ate eleven. In the Polaroid, taken before a handwritten calendar in the fire chief's office, he's still asleep. Dwight says it's the best one he took all day. Getting a good picture of Lonnie usually involves asking him to quit talking; this was a hell of a shortcut.

Roy Stubblefield's red cap is in the left edge. He was next.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0031 — Roy Stubblefield "Chief": Operating a tree lot without a permit; assault with a Scotch pine
item.description: Roy Stubblefield opened his Christmas tree lot at the old Sinclair station at 5 a.m. He believes people buying trees at 5 a.m. don't haggle. He's right. Anybody shopping for a pine in the dark has other shit going on.
item.content:encoded:
Roy Stubblefield opened his Christmas tree lot at the old Sinclair station at 5 a.m. He believes people buying trees at 5 a.m. don't haggle. He's right. Anybody shopping for a pine in the dark has other shit going on.

Roy had no permit. He had a Chiefs cap, a horseshoe mustache, and a policy. Around here that's most of a business plan.

Deputy Hargrove stopped for a tree. Asked friendly enough to see the permit. Roy asked, considerably less friendly, whether he wanted a tree or a conversation.

"Both."

Roy handed him a seven-foot Scotch pine at a speed the Deputy's report described as "thrown." Hargrove had come intending to spend money with Roy, too. Two fellas trying to have Christmas, and now one had the damn thing coming at his head.

"It's a Christmas tree," Roy said from the back of the cruiser. "You can't assault a man with Christmas."

You sure as hell can. It's needles. The holiday don't round them off.

Dwight shot him under the NO SMOKING sign, serious as a hymn. God love Roy, he looked ready to argue the case clear up to whoever was in charge of pine trees.

His nephew ran the lot the rest of the day and sold out by three. He haggled. Roy's policy wasn't worth a damn without Roy there to throw it.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0030 — Bonnie Threlkeld "Bingo Bonnie": Filing a false report; theft by deception (bingo prizes)
item.description: Bonnie Threlkeld called in the nacho cart theft at 4:20 a.m. and gave particulars fit for a deposition. Tammy Jo Carter had wheeled it out the side door of the bingo hall. True as could be. Bonnie just left out who'd unlocked the door, turned off the alarm, and filled the cart.
item.content:encoded:
Bonnie Threlkeld called in the nacho cart theft at 4:20 a.m. and gave particulars fit for a deposition. Tammy Jo Carter had wheeled it out the side door of the bingo hall. True as could be. Bonnie just left out who'd unlocked the door, turned off the alarm, and filled the cart.

Bonnie had. Woman had done every damn thing but get there first.

She runs Saturday bingo the way Vegas runs Vegas. Six of the last eight blackout jackpots went to her sister, her other sister, and "R. Threlkeld," a man who does not exist. Family resemblance must be hell to establish on that last one.

Deputy Hargrove might've spent all morning sorting it out, except Bonnie, in her floral blouse and big rounded glasses, explaining the theft, said, "before I could get it out myself."

There's your loose board. Stepped right through it.

"Before you could what, Bonnie?"

"Well, shit."

I reckon we've all wished we could reach across a desk and put a sentence back in our mouth. Hers just came with a nacho cart attached.

In the Polaroid her head's tilted. Still figuring whether she actually said that, or whether Hargrove might could have heard some entirely different bullshit.

She said it. When they finally caught Tammy Jo, she called Bonnie "a real one."

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0029 — Jesse Rademacher: Peace disturbance; unlicensed serenade
item.description: Jesse Rademacher stood outside Tammy Jo Carter's trailer at 4:15 a.m., holding a boom box over his head like Cusack. He was playing "The Dance" by Garth Brooks, plaid shirt open to the chest in weather colder than a well-digger's ass.
item.content:encoded:
Jesse Rademacher stood outside Tammy Jo Carter's trailer at 4:15 a.m., holding a boom box over his head like Cusack. He was playing "The Dance" by Garth Brooks, plaid shirt open to the chest in weather colder than a well-digger's ass.

Tammy Jo wasn't home. She was across town stealing a nacho cart from the bingo hall. Jesse had picked a hell of a night to demonstrate how much he could carry.

He serenaded that dark trailer for fifty minutes. Neighbors called at twenty. Deputy Stotts arrived at forty and sat in the cruiser till the song finished. It's a good song. She wasn't about to ruin the only part of this mess that was going right.

"She's not in there, Jesse."

"I know it."

"Then who's the song for?"

He thought on that. "The trailer's heard some things."

Well, shit. You can put a man in a warm car. There ain't a form for the rest of it.

He rode in with the boom box on his lap. In the Polaroid his necklace has a tiny gold nacho pendant. Tammy Jo had it made for him at the county fair in August, before everything went to hell with the cart. Little bitty nacho. He still wore the damn thing right over his heart.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0028 — Travis Oakes: Stealing (one Santa suit); attempted felony chimney entry
item.description: Travis Oakes is nineteen, youngest of eight, and has never gotten what he asked for at Christmas. By the eighth kid, Santa's just dumping whatever's left in the damn sack. This year Travis figured he'd handle distribution himself.
item.content:encoded:
Travis Oakes is nineteen, youngest of eight, and has never gotten what he asked for at Christmas. By the eighth kid, Santa's just dumping whatever's left in the damn sack. This year Travis figured he'd handle distribution himself.

At 4 a.m. they found him on Walmart's roof in a Santa suit he'd shoplifted from that same Walmart Wednesday, halfway into an HVAC duct. He didn't think it was a chimney. Give the boy that much. He thought it went to Electronics.

It went to the deli. Hell of a place to shop for a stereo.

He'd left a note on his Cavalier's windshield: “Gone to work. -T.” Deputy Hargrove considered that a confession. Around here a boy finally shows some initiative and the paperwork eats his ass.

Dwight took the Polaroid at the fingerprint shelf. Striped shirt, forearm on the counter, calm as a fellow waiting on biscuits. Underneath you can see the boot of another guy, asleep, been there since two. God love Travis, he looks willing to wait his turn.

The suit's in evidence. Walmart wants it back. There's a mayonnaise situation. Nobody wants to explain that shit to the returns lady.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0027 — Cody Whitlow: Indecent exposure; attempted baptism without clergy
item.description: Cody Whitlow got saved at 3:30 in the morning, which ain't regular church hours, but Cody wasn't having a regular damn evening. Nobody witnessed it but him. He says that was the point.
item.content:encoded:
Cody Whitlow got saved at 3:30 in the morning, which ain't regular church hours, but Cody wasn't having a regular damn evening. Nobody witnessed it but him. He says that was the point.

He left the Rusty Nail with a clear conscience and a cloudy everything else, walked eleven blocks to First Baptist, and used the side door they never lock because of the Christmas pageant. Climbed into the baptistry in his jeans. Thought on that. Climbed out of his jeans. A man hates to get to heaven in wet denim.

On his fourth full immersion he was telling the ceiling, “I got it, I got it,” when Sheriff Ponder came to check on a light.

“Cody. Son. There's a process.”

“I'm doing the process. Hell, I'm doing it four times.”

“There's a pastor in the process.”

“Well, he ain't here. I am.”

Cody's shirt was never found. The Sheriff brought him in with a choir robe on his lap and the heater going, because salvation is one thing and freezing your ass off is another. God love him, Cody looked relieved enough for both of them.

In the Polaroid he's shirtless, wet-haired, staring straight into the lens. Square with the Lord. Just county bullshit left to handle.

Brother Dale says it counts. He's not happy about it, but it counts.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0026 — Dustin Kroger "Dusty": Vandalism; unlawful posting of bills
item.description: Dusty Kroger walked into the Sheriff's Office at 3:10 a.m. a free man, carrying enough band flyers to correct that oversight. He'd come to bail out his cousin Shane and the deer.
item.content:encoded:
Dusty Kroger walked into the Sheriff's Office at 3:10 a.m. a free man, carrying enough band flyers to correct that oversight. He'd come to bail out his cousin Shane and the deer.

Waiting by the bulletin board, he got bored. In his coat he had flyers for Dusty & the Kroger Brothers, playing the VFW Christmas dance that night. Seemed a shame to waste good wall space on fellas who weren't even coming.

He pinned a flyer over every wanted poster. Neatly, too. Used their own pins. Dusty would never leave you short a pin, bless his heart, even while covering up your whole damn manhunt.

Dwight came back from the Coke machine. Seventeen fugitives had become seventeen Dustys.

"You covered up a murderer, Dusty."

"He's got the whole rest of the state. We got one goddamn dance."

"This ain't a booking agency."

It was fixin' to be one, though.

Dwight booked him right there in his own lobby, navy shirt and mullet and all. The Polaroid shows a Dusty & the Kroger Brothers flyer over his left shoulder. Free publicity, if you weren't particular about the charge underneath.

Shane and the deer waited another four hours. Hell of a favor to do your cousin. The band went on at nine. We love Dusty. They sounded like shit.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0025 — Shane Lockridge: Careless and imprudent driving; transport of a deer, unfield-dressed, in a passenger seat
item.description: Deer camp broke up at midnight, and Shane Lockridge drove home with a ten-point buck riding shotgun, upright, seatbelted, wearing Shane's Cardinals cap. Most folks take home meat. Shane took home somebody to split the driving.
item.content:encoded:
Deer camp broke up at midnight, and Shane Lockridge drove home with a ten-point buck riding shotgun, upright, seatbelted, wearing Shane's Cardinals cap. Most folks take home meat. Shane took home somebody to split the driving.

“For the checkpoint,” he said. There wasn't a damn checkpoint. There was Deputy Hargrove, who stopped him on Highway 5 for doing thirty-one in a fifty-five with his flashers on. That's the speed of a man transporting either dynamite or a covered dish he can't replace.

Shane wore a black tank top in thirty-one-degree weather and a necklace that had belonged to somebody else. God love him, he'd dressed the deer better than himself.

“His name's Gerald. He's seen things.”

“Shane, where the hell is your shirt?”

“Gerald's wearing it.”

Gerald was. Couldn't argue that part. The buck looked ready to help somebody move a couch, except for being dead and full of deer.

Shane's got a little half-smile in the Polaroid. He knows Gerald's still in the truck. He also knows who ain't fixin' to haul that heavy son of a bitch out of there: anybody present.

Nobody did. Gerald sat in impound till Sunday noon, the best-dressed thing in the lot. Shirt, cap, seatbelt. Had his shit together better than most of us.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0024 — Homer Stroud: Misfiled (Henry County, 09 28 96); a future Homer
item.description: The third Henry County photo is dated September 28, 1996. Ten months from now. Well, shit. Most counties can't file yesterday right; this one's already disappointed in next September.
item.content:encoded:
The third Henry County photo is dated September 28, 1996. Ten months from now. Well, shit. Most counties can't file yesterday right; this one's already disappointed in next September.

Homer Stroud. Fifty-some, cap and plaid shirt, two unsmiling views, holding a slate for something he ain't done yet.

Dwight held it up to the cell at 2:40 a.m. "Anybody know a Homer?" Everybody did. Everybody knows a Homer. This particular Homer was the difficulty.

Norman Petrie, Legion adjutant, eating his own raffled ham through the bars, said, "That's Homer Stroud. From Clinton. He does gutters."

"Has he been arrested?"

"Not yet."

"It says September."

Norman studied it. "Well, hell. He's gonna be." Then back to his ham. A man can only worry about so much on an empty fork.

So Homer Stroud does gutters in Clinton, hasn't done whatever he's fixin' to do, and his picture sits in the Ponder County December 2 stack anyhow. God love him, he's getting a head start on a bad day.

The Sheriff called Clinton on Monday, got Homer himself, asked was everything all right. Homer said yes, why. The Sheriff said no reason, hung up, and sat there. What the damn hell do you warn a man against? September?

Dwight says it's the only Polaroid in the stack that's "still developing."

All persons and events are fiction.
